title: Moving Day
blurb: Today you're moving your mum into a new ground-floor flat — she can't manage the stairs any more, and it all has to be done before dark. With the van running late, a removal man ramping up his price, and a box of your dad's things gone missing, you have one short afternoon to get her home honestly — and to decide who you let carry the load with you.

identity.name: Home by Dark
identity.mood: The last day in the old place and the first in the new; boxes, bare rooms, and a short autumn afternoon to get your mum home before dark.

cover.alt: A small removal van at the kerb at dusk, its back open and boxes on the wet pavement, with a warm-lit doorway and a figure carrying a box toward it.

line.en: You're moving your mum into a new place today, and the light is going. Get her home before dark — the honest way, with whoever will carry it with you.
line.fr: Aujourd'hui, tu installes ta mère dans un nouveau logement, et le jour baisse. Ramène-la chez elle avant la nuit — honnêtement, avec ceux qui voudront bien porter avec toi.
line.es: Hoy trasladas a tu madre a un piso nuevo, y la luz se va. Llévala a casa antes de que anochezca, de forma honrada, con quien quiera cargar contigo.
line.it: Oggi trasferisci tua madre in una casa nuova, e la luce se ne va. Portala a casa prima del buio, in modo onesto, con chi vorrà portare il peso con te.
line.de: Heute ziehst du deine Mutter in eine neue Wohnung, und das Licht schwindet. Bring sie vor der Dunkelheit heim — ehrlich, mit allen, die mit dir tragen wollen.
line.pt: Hoje mudas a tua mãe para uma casa nova, e a luz está a ir-se. Leva-a a casa antes de escurecer, de forma honesta, com quem quiser carregar contigo.
line.ru: Сегодня ты перевозишь маму в новую квартиру, и свет уходит. Успей привезти её домой до темноты — честно, с теми, кто готов нести это вместе с тобой.
line.zh: 今天你要把妈妈搬进新家，而天色正在暗下来。赶在天黑前把她安顿好——用正当的法子，和愿意陪你一起扛的人。
line.ar: اليوم تنقل أمك إلى بيت جديد، والضوء يخبو. أوصلها إلى البيت قبل حلول الظلام — بطريقة نزيهة، مع كل من يريد أن يحمل الحمل معك.

text.B2: It's gone two o'clock, and the light will fade by five. Today you move your mum, Edie, into her new ground-floor flat. She can't manage the stairs in this old place any more. She sits among the half-packed boxes, waiting, her hands folded in her lap. The van is late, the new key is stiff in the lock, and one box has already gone missing. For the first time, getting her home before dark is all on you.

text.A2: You look at what's left to move. Mum's bed and her big chair, the last of the boxes, a few bags. But the box with your dad's things isn't where you left it. It's gone three now, and the light is turning. You have to decide what to do, and move fast.

You have to decide what to do, and you have to move fast.

text.A2: You call an old mate to ask for a hand. The phone rings and rings. Then he picks up. He can't come — he's away for the day. But he talks you through it, calm. 'Load the heavy stuff low,' he says. 'Little and often. You'll get there.' And somehow you start to believe him.

text.B2: You call an old mate to ask for a hand. The phone rings and rings, and then at last he picks up. He can't come over — he's away for the whole day. But he talks you through it anyway, calm and clear. 'Load the heavy stuff low,' he says. 'Little and often, and mind your back. You'll get there.' And somehow, hearing him, you start to believe it.

text.A2: You go to Mum first. You make her tea and settle her in her chair. 'Don't fuss over me,' she says, but her hand holds yours. The rooms are still full, though, and the light is going. Sitting with her won't shift the boxes. You need a plan, and a clear head, before you start.

text.A2: You roll up your sleeves and start to load. You lift one box, then another, and find a rhythm. Outside, the light is going grey. Then a van pulls up and a man leans out. 'Need a hand with that lot?' he calls. 'Cheap, cash, done by dark.' You weren't expecting anyone.

You weren't expecting anyone, not yet, and something about him puts you on your guard.

text.A2: You make yourself stop and think. You could start carrying down right now and sort the rest later. You could load the heavy things first. Or you could knock on doors and ask for a hand. Each choice costs time you don't have. And the light keeps going.

text.A2: The weight of it presses down on you. You think of Mum in her chair, of the dark coming, of the key you can't yet turn. A whole new start rests on this one afternoon. That isn't a worry; it's a plain fact. No one else will carry it in for you. It's you, today, or it waits.

text.A2: On the stairs, you hear a call. An old woman is stuck with her shopping — two heavy bags, no lift, bad knees. She can't get them up, and no one stops. 'Could you?' she asks. You've a flat to fill before dark. But she's right here, stuck, and asking you.

text.A2: You knock round the doors, asking the same thing each time. Can you lend a hand? Take an end of the sofa. Carry a box. Mind Mum for ten minutes. Some say no — busy, tired, bad back. But a few say yes, and come down. Today, a few is enough.

text.A2: You take charge of the move. You sort it all out: heavy and low, light on top, Mum's things kept safe and apart. Done well, this gets her home in one trip. Rushed or jumbled, and something breaks on the stairs. So you take a breath and load it right, with care.

text.A2: Old Tom from the ground floor has moved more homes than he can count. 'Don't carry too much to save trips,' he says. 'That's how backs go, and boxes.' He warns you about Bray too, the man with the van. 'Do it yourself, slow and steady. That's the whole job today.'

text.A2: You help the man lift the box and carry it to his door. He catches his breath. 'Here,' he says, and presses a key into your hand. It opens the back gate, so you can bring the van close. 'Saves your legs,' he says. A small thing, freely given, and you take it and go on.
text.B1: You help the man lift the box and carry it to his door. He catches his breath. 'Here,' he says, and presses a key into your hand. It opens the back gate, so you can bring the van right up close. 'Saves your legs,' he says. A small thing — but freely given, and you take it and go on.
text.B2: You help the man lift the box and carry it the last few feet to his door. He catches his breath, leaning on the frame. 'Here,' he says, and presses a key into your hand. It opens the back gate, so you can bring the van right up to the stairs. 'Saves your legs,' he says, with a tired nod. A small thing — but freely given, and you take it and go on your way.

text.A2: You can't stop now — but you can't just leave him, either. So you promise to send help soon. 'Hang on,' you say. 'Catch your breath — I'll send someone down.' You mean it, too. And then you turn and carry on.
text.B1: You can't stop now — but you can't just leave him, either. So you promise to send help soon. 'Hang on,' you say. 'Catch your breath — I'll send someone down to you.' You mean it, too. And then you turn and carry on.
text.B2: You can't stop now — but you can't simply leave him, either. So you promise to send help soon. 'Hang on,' you say, over your shoulder. 'Catch your breath — I'll send someone down to you.' You mean it, too; and then you turn and carry on up the stairs, carrying the weight of it.

text.A2: You get one good thing going — you set up a chain on the stairs. One hands a box down, the next takes it, the next stacks it in the van. People breathe easier. It isn't the whole move. But it's real, and it's a good start.
text.B1: You get one good thing going — you set up a steady chain on the stairs. One hands a box down, the next takes it, the next stacks it in the van. People breathe easier. It isn't the whole move. But it's real, and it's a good start.
text.B2: You get one good thing going — you set up a steady chain on the stairs. One hands a box down, the next takes it, the next stacks it tight in the van. People breathe easier with a system. It isn't the whole move, not by a long way. But it's real, and it's a good start, and the stairwell hums with it.

text.A2: Hand by hand, the panic turns into a working chain. Everyone has a job now: one lifts, one carries, one packs the van tight. Worry turns into doing. And doing beats worrying, every time. The stairwell fills with footsteps and quiet, steady work.
text.B1: Hand by hand, the panic turns into a working chain. Everyone has a job now: one lifts, one carries, one packs the van tight. Worry turns into doing. And doing beats worrying, every single time. The stairwell fills with footsteps and quiet, steady work.
text.B2: Hand by hand, box by box, the panic turns into a working chain. Everyone has a job now: one lifts, one carries down, one packs the van tight. Worry turns into doing — and doing beats worrying, on a moving day, every single time. The stairwell fills with footsteps and quiet, steady work, and the worst of the panic lifts.

text.A2: The long afternoon wears at you. A voice says: give up, leave the rest, finish tomorrow. No one would blame you, and it would be easy. But you think of Mum, home before dark. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while there's light.
text.B1: The long afternoon wears at you. A small voice says: give up, leave the rest, finish tomorrow — no one would blame you, and it would be so easy. But you think of Mum, home before dark. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while there's still light.
text.B2: The long afternoon wears at you. A small voice says: give up, leave the rest, finish it tomorrow — no one would blame you, and it would be so easy to do. But you think of Mum, home and settled before dark. And you push the voice away. Not yet. Not while there's still light in the sky.

text.A2: You sit on a step a moment. You check the list of what's left. Half of it is done; the hard half isn't. You could push on and clear the rest. Or something makes you look down the stairs — and there, at the door, a face you half know.
text.B1: You sit on a step a moment and check the list of what's left. Half of it is done; the hard half isn't. You could push on and clear the rest. Or something makes you look down the stairs — and there, at the door below, a face you half know.
text.B2: You sit on a step a moment and check the list of what's left to shift. Half of it is done; the hard, heavy half isn't. You could push on and clear the rest before dark. Or something makes you look down the stairs — and there, at the door below, a face you half know, half dread.

text.A2: Bray leans on the van, all friendly. 'Tell you what,' he says. 'I'll take the lot — stairs, heavy bits, all of it, done in half an hour. Put your feet up. Why do your back in?' His smile is wide. But his eyes are already on your stuff.
text.B1: Bray leans on the van, all friendly. 'Tell you what,' he says. 'I'll take the lot — stairs, heavy bits, all of it, done in half an hour. Just put your feet up. Why do your back in?' His smile is wide. But his eyes are already on your stuff.
text.B2: Bray leans on the van, all friendly. 'Tell you what,' he says. 'I'll take the whole lot — stairs, heavy bits, all of it, done in half an hour flat. Just say the word and put your feet up. Why do your back in?' His smile is wide and easy. But his eyes are already running over your stuff, pricing it up.

text.A2: 'Good price,' Bray says, and names a sum that makes you blink. It's a lot. But he's quick, he's strong, and he's right here. No stairs, no strain, no risk to your back. So: pay him, turn him down, or ask him straight what his game is?
text.B1: 'Good price,' Bray says, and names a sum that makes you blink. It's a lot of money. But he's quick, he's strong, and he's right here in front of you. No stairs, no strain, no risk to your back. So what's it to be — pay him, turn him down, or ask what his game is?
text.B2: 'Good price,' Bray says, and names a sum that makes you blink. It's a lot of money, more than you'd budgeted. But he's quick, he's strong, and he's right here in front of you now. No stairs, no strain, no risk to your bad back. So what's it to be — pay him, turn him down flat, or ask him straight out what his game really is?

text.A2: You say no thanks and turn back to the boxes. It feels good to turn him down. He calls after you, but you don't look round. His sort always find someone. But it won't be you, not today.
text.B1: You say no thanks and turn back to the boxes. It feels good to turn him down. He calls something after you, but you don't look round. His sort always find someone, in the end. But it won't be you, not today.
text.B2: You say no thanks and turn back to the boxes. It feels good to turn him down flat. He calls something after you, but you don't look round. His sort always find someone, in the end — someone tired and stuck enough. But it won't be you, not today. You go back to the stairs, and the honest work.

text.A2: You shake on it and hand over the cash. The notes leave your hand, and part of you already knows. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart. It feels like a small mistake, just starting.
text.B1: You shake on it and hand over the cash. The notes leave your hand, and part of you already knows. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart at all. It feels like a small mistake, just starting.
text.B2: You shake on it and hand over the cash. The notes leave your hand, and part of you already knows the truth of it. His smile grows. 'Smart move,' he says. But it doesn't feel smart at all. It feels, standing there, like a small mistake being made — one you'll be paying for all evening.

text.A2: You ask him straight: why so keen to help? He laughs. 'Easy money, love,' he says. 'Folk in a fix pay whatever I ask.' He laughs again. At least he's honest — and that tells you all you need to know.
text.B1: You ask him straight: why is he so keen to help? He laughs. 'Easy money, love,' he says. 'Folk in a fix pay whatever I ask.' He laughs again. At least he's honest — and that tells you all you need to know.
text.B2: You ask him straight out: why is he so keen to help? He laughs, quite openly. 'Easy money, love,' he says. 'Folk in a fix pay whatever I ask, don't they.' He laughs again. At least he's honest — and that, right there, tells you everything you need to know.

text.A2: You let Bray load the van his way. But he throws it in fast and rough. Boxes on their sides, Mum's chair wedged under the heavy stuff. Nothing's safe in there. The whole thing already feels like a mistake.
text.B1: You let Bray load the van his way. But he throws it in fast and rough — boxes on their sides, Mum's chair wedged under the heavy stuff. Nothing's safe in there. The whole thing already feels like a mistake.
text.B2: You let Bray load the van his own way. But he throws it in fast and rough — boxes on their sides, Mum's good chair wedged under the heavy stuff. Nothing's safe in there at all. The whole thing already feels, in your stomach, like a mistake. You should have loaded it yourself.

text.A2: Off to the new place with it.
text.B1: Off to the new place with it.
text.B2: Off to the new place with it.

text.A2: You look in the van, and your heart sinks. He's piled it in anyhow — glass boxes under the wardrobe, Mum's lamp on its side. Nothing will come out whole. You paid good money for this, and it's not worth it. The bad feeling in your gut was right.
text.B1: You look in the van, and your heart sinks. He's piled it in anyhow — glass boxes under the wardrobe, Mum's lamp on its side. Nothing will come out whole. You paid good money for this, and it's not worth it. The bad feeling in your gut was right all along.
text.B2: You look in the back of the van, and your heart sinks. He's piled it in anyhow — glass boxes crushed under the wardrobe, Mum's good lamp on its side. Nothing in there will come out whole. You paid good money for this, and it's not worth it. The bad feeling in your gut was right about him all along.

text.A2: You turn to stop him, but Bray's already pulling away, your deposit in his pocket. He was never really helping. He saw someone stuck and in a hurry, and he cashed in. You've been had, plain and simple.
text.B1: You turn to stop him, but Bray's already pulling away, your deposit in his pocket. He was never really helping you. He saw someone stuck and in a hurry, and he cashed in. You've been had, plain and simple.
text.B2: You turn to stop him, but Bray's already pulling away from the kerb, your deposit in his pocket. He was never really helping you at all. He saw someone stuck and in a hurry, and he cashed in on it. You've been had, out here, plain and simple. The dusk settles, and the van's gone.

text.A2: He's gone, and the kerb is empty. Just the dusk now, and the money you handed him for nothing. You learned something today. And you paid too much for it. Now you carry on with less than you had.
text.B1: He's gone, and the kerb is empty — just the dusk now, and the money you handed him for nothing. You learned something today. And you paid far too much for it. Now you carry on with less than you started with.
text.B2: He's gone, and the kerb is empty — just the dusk now, the cold, and the money you handed him for nothing at all. You learned something today, out here. And you paid far too much for it. Now you carry on with less than you started with, and the light no kinder.

text.A2: Stand a moment at the kerb.
text.B1: Stand a moment at the kerb.
text.B2: Stand a moment at the kerb.

text.A2: Other tired movers are paying Bray too — cash in hand, glad to put their feet up. He takes it slow, with that same smile. He only ever helps the ones who pay the most.
text.B1: Other tired movers are paying Bray too — cash in hand, glad to put their feet up. He takes it slow, with that same smile. He only ever helps the ones who can pay the most.
text.B2: Other tired movers are paying Bray too — cash in hand, glad of any chance to put their feet up today. He takes it slow, unhurried, with that same wide smile. He only ever helps the ones who can pay him the most — and you see the whole of him in it.

text.A2: You're halfway up the stairs now, the pile swaying in your arms. The landing looks close — or does it? You can't see the steps past the boxes. And you're a long way up, with no free hand.
text.B1: You're halfway up the stairs now, the pile swaying in your arms. The landing looks close — or does it? You can't see the steps past the boxes. And you're a long way up, with no free hand to grab the rail.
text.B2: You're halfway up the stairs now, the whole pile swaying in your arms. The landing looks close — or does it? You can't see the steps at all past the boxes. And you're a long way up, with no free hand to grab the rail if you slip. You keep climbing, and you do not look down.

text.A2: The top box slides, and the whole pile lurches. This is the moment. You can grab for it and hope you keep your feet. Or you can let it go and save yourself, while you still can.
text.B1: The top box slides, and the whole pile lurches. This is the moment. You can grab for it and hope you keep your feet. Or you can let it go and save yourself, while you still can.
text.B2: The top box slides, and the whole pile lurches in your arms. This is the moment, and it's a short one. You can grab for it and hope you keep your feet on the steps. Or you can let the lot go and save yourself, right now, while you still can.

text.A2: You reach the landing at last, arms shaking, heart going hard — but up. Somehow you made it. Now you must choose. Push on, shaken as you are? Or go back down for what you dropped on the stairs?
text.B1: You reach the landing at last, arms shaking, heart going hard — but up. Somehow you made it. Now you have to decide: push on, shaken as you are, or go back down for what you dropped on the stairs.
text.B2: You reach the landing at last, your arms shaking, your heart going hard against your ribs — but up. Somehow, against the odds, you made it. Now you have to decide: push on, shaken as you are, or go back down for the box you dropped on the stairs. Either way, the light will not wait.

text.A2: You let the pile go and step clear just in time — the hard, right choice. The boxes tumble down; you stay on your feet. You're shaken, but whole. The move isn't lost. But you've lost time you'll miss — and you'll do it one at a time now.
text.B1: You let the pile go and step clear just in time — the hard, right choice. The boxes tumble down the stairs; you stay on your feet. You're shaken, but whole. The move isn't lost. But you've lost time you'll miss — and you'll do it one at a time now.
text.B2: You let the whole pile go and step clear just in time — the hard choice, and the right one. The boxes tumble down the stairs; you stay on your feet. You're shaken, but whole, and nothing of Mum's is broken. The move isn't lost. But you've lost time you'll badly miss — and you'll do it one at a time now, like you should have.

text.A2: You try to help the young mum get started. Tape a box, take the baby a minute, shift the heavy things to the door. It helps a little. But she's barely begun, and you can't stay long. There's really only one thing you can do for her.
text.B1: You try to help the young mum get started — tape a box, take the baby a minute, shift the heavy things to the door. It helps a little. But she's barely begun, and you can't stay long. There's really only one thing you can do for her.
text.B2: You try to help the young mum get started — tape up a box, hold the baby a minute, shift the heavy things over to the door. It helps a little. But she's barely begun, and you can't stay long today. There's really only one thing left that you can do for her.

text.A2: Lend her your van and hands.
text.B1: Lend her your van and hands.
text.B2: Lend her your van and hands.

text.A2: You run her boxes down in your van alongside your own, and her face changes. Two trips become one. The weight lifts off her. 'Thank you,' she says — then she tells you someone's been asking for you, downstairs.
text.B1: You run her boxes down in your van alongside your own, and her face changes. Two trips become one. The weight lifts off her. 'Thank you,' she says — and then she tells you that someone's been asking for you, downstairs.
text.B2: You run her boxes down in your van alongside your own, and her tired face changes all at once. Two trips become one. The weight lifts clean off her. 'Thank you,' she says, over and over — and then she tells you that someone's been asking for you, downstairs, by name.

text.A2: With her load shifted too, your own time is tighter. Now the light is lower and the van's half yours. You helped because you could, and you'd do it again. But the dusk doesn't care about that. It just keeps falling.
text.B1: With her load shifted too, your own time is tighter. Now the light is lower and the van's half hers. You helped because you could, and you'd do it again. But the dusk doesn't care about any of that. It just keeps falling.
text.B2: With her load shifted too, your own time is that much tighter. Now the light is lower and the van's half hers. You helped because you could, and you'd do it again in a heartbeat. But the dusk doesn't care about any of that. It just keeps falling toward dark.

text.A2: A neighbour calls you in for tea.
text.B1: A neighbour calls you in for tea.
text.B2: A neighbour calls you in for tea.

text.A2: A neighbour waves you in for a cup of tea. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, warm up, catch your breath.' The room is warm. Your aching back begs you to stop. But five minutes can turn into twenty.
text.B1: A neighbour waves you in for a cup of tea. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, warm up, catch your breath.' It's warm and dry inside, and your aching back begs you to stop. But five minutes like this can quietly turn into twenty.
text.B2: A neighbour waves you in for a cup of tea out of the cold. 'Just five minutes,' they say. 'Sit down, warm up, catch your breath.' It's warm and dry in there, and your aching back begs you to stop a while. But five minutes like this one can quietly turn into twenty, with the light going.

text.A2: You press on in the cooling dusk. Your arms are sore, your back stiff, the light in your head. Each box is a small effort now. But you keep them coming, one after another, toward the new flat and home.
text.B1: You press on in the cooling dusk, arms sore, your back stiff, the fading light in your head. Each box is a small effort now. But you keep them coming, one after another, toward the new flat and home.
text.B2: You press on in the cooling dusk, your arms sore, your back stiff, the fading light loud in your head. Each box is a small effort on its own now. But you keep them coming, one after another after another, toward the new flat and home. You will not stop until it's done.

text.A2: A neighbour stops you. 'There's a lad round the back,' she says. 'On his own with a wardrobe, about to drop it. No one's helping.' Round the corner, a young man leans against the weight, going red. If no one lends a hand, it'll come down on him.
text.B1: A neighbour stops you. 'There's a lad round the back,' she says, 'struggling with a wardrobe on his own, about to drop it. No one's helping.' Round the corner, a young man leans against the weight, going red in the face. If no one lends a hand, it'll come down on him.
text.B2: A neighbour stops you. 'There's a lad round the back,' she says, 'struggling with a wardrobe all on his own, about to drop it. No one's helping.' Round the corner, a young man leans against the weight of it, going red in the face. If no one lends a hand now, it'll come down on top of him.

text.A2: You get a shoulder under the wardrobe just in time. Together you lower it safe. He's shaking, out of breath, too winded to speak. 'Easy,' you say. 'I've got this end. Let's set it down.' And slowly the weight comes off you both.
text.B1: You get a shoulder under the wardrobe just in time. Together you lower it down safe. He's shaking, out of breath, too winded to speak. 'Easy,' you say. 'I've got this end. Let's set it down.' And slowly the weight comes off you both.
text.B2: You get a shoulder under the wardrobe just in time. Together, straining, you lower it down safe. He's shaking, out of breath, too winded to speak. 'Easy,' you say, steady. 'I've got this end. Let's set it down slow.' And slowly the weight comes off the two of you.

text.A2: You can't do it all at once, and Mum's move needs you most. So you call over a couple of the others to take the weight, and press on. It sits badly with you. But today you have to choose, and keep on choosing.
text.B1: You can't do it all at once, and Mum's move needs you most of all. So you call over a couple of the others to take the weight, and press on. It sits badly with you. But today you have to choose, and keep on choosing.

text.A2: You help him walk the wardrobe to his door and set it down. His face fills with relief. His mates crowd round and clap you on the back. 'Thanks, pal,' they keep saying. But your own van's waiting, and you can't stay long.
text.B1: You help him walk the wardrobe to his door and set it down. His face fills with relief. His mates crowd round and clap you on the back. 'Thanks, pal,' they keep saying to you. But your own van's waiting, and you can't stay long today.
text.B2: You help him walk the wardrobe to his door and set it down at last. His face fills with relief at the sight. His mates crowd round and clap you on the back. 'Thanks, pal,' they keep saying to you, over and over. But your own van's waiting at the kerb, and you can't stay long today.

text.A2: To the new place at last.
text.B1: To the new place at last.
text.B2: To the new place at last.

text.A2: You stop a moment and look down the street. Movers and cars go by, everyone busy, everyone in their own day. The light is nearly gone. Only one person stands still at your gate, looking up. Something about them stops your breath.
text.B1: You stop a moment and look down the street. Movers and cars go by, everyone busy, everyone in their own day. The light is nearly gone now. Only one person stands still at your gate, looking up. Something about them stops your breath.
text.B2: You stop a moment and look down the street. Movers and cars go by, everyone busy, everyone wrapped up in their own day. The light is nearly gone now. Only one person stands quite still at your gate, looking up at the flat. And something about them, something you can't name, stops your breath.

text.A2: The work turns as hard as it gets now. Your arms are dead, your back aches, your legs won't lift. It's hard to think, hard to carry, hard to care. The last boxes feel like stone. This is the worst of it.
text.B1: The work turns as hard as it gets now. Your arms are dead, your back aches, your legs won't lift. It's hard to think, hard to carry, hard to care. The last boxes feel like stone in your hands. This is the worst of it — the hardest part of the whole day.

The last boxes feel like stone in your hands. This is the worst of it — the hardest part of the whole long day.

text.A2: Old Reg presses something on you — a proper sack trolley from the store cupboard. 'For the heavy stuff,' he says. 'Go on, take it. Saves your back the worst of it.' His face is kind in the stairwell light. It's what he has to give today, and he gives it gladly.
text.B1: Old Reg presses something on you — a proper sack trolley from the store cupboard. 'For the heavy stuff,' he says. 'Go on, take it. Saves your back the worst of it.' His face is kind in the stairwell light. It's what he has to give today, and he gives all of it gladly.
text.B2: Old Reg presses something on you — a proper sack trolley from the store cupboard. 'For the heavy stuff,' he says. 'Go on, take it. It'll save your back the worst of it.' His face is kind in the stairwell light. It's what he has to give today, and he gives every bit of it gladly.

text.A2: Ask what else to watch for.
text.B1: Ask what else to watch for.
text.B2: Ask what else to watch for.

text.A2: At the van, people are grabbing for space — your boxes, the mum's, a neighbour's bags, all at once. Voices rise, arms reach, it's getting fraught. One more shove and something breaks. You can try to calm it and pack it fair. Or you can get your own in and go.

text.B2: At the van, people are grabbing for space — your boxes, the young mum's, a neighbour's bags, all at once. Voices rise, arms reach across each other, it's getting fraught. text.A2: A quiet spot by the back gate, where the noise falls away. You stop to breathe. Then you see her — by the wall, half-turned, achingly familiar. Someone you knew all your life, and lost. Your heart goes still.
text.B1: A quiet spot by the back gate, where the noise falls away. You stop to breathe for a moment. Then you see her — by the wall, half-turned, achingly familiar. Someone you knew all your life, and lost. Your heart goes still.
text.B2: A quiet spot by the back gate, where the noise falls away to almost nothing. You stop a moment just to breathe. Then you see her — standing by the wall, half-turned, achingly familiar. Someone you knew all your life, and grew up beside, and lost. And your heart goes quite still in your chest.

text.A2: At the gate, a figure stands where the light is thin. They seem to be looking right at you — then away, then back. You can't place them, and yet you can. Something in you needs to know. And something in you is afraid to.
text.B1: At the gate, a figure stands where the light is thin. They seem to be looking right at you — then away, then back again. You can't place them, and yet you can. Something in you needs to know. And something in you is afraid to.
text.B2: At the gate, a figure stands where the light is thin. They seem to be looking right at you — then away, then back again, slowly. You can't quite place them, and yet somehow you can. Something in you needs to know who it is. And something in you, just as strong, is afraid to.

text.A2: You cross the yard toward them and lift a hand. They don't move, or don't let on. Then you catch their face in the last light — and the years fall away. You know that face. You've known it your whole life.
text.B1: You cross the yard toward them and lift a hand. They don't move, or don't let on. Then you catch their face in the last of the light — and the years fall away. You know that face. You've known it your whole life.
text.B2: You cross the yard toward them and lift a hand. They don't move, or don't choose to let on. Then you catch their face in the last of the light — and all the years fall away at once. You know that face. You've known it your whole life. And your feet carry you on toward it.

text.A2: You reach her, and your heart turns over. It's Cass — your sister, older now, the same tired eyes, a bag at her feet. She came. The one you fell out with, years ago, and never put right. No time to think. You have to speak now.
text.B1: You reach her, and your heart turns over. It's Cass — your sister, older now, the same tired eyes, a bag at her feet. She came. The one you fell out with, years ago, and never put right. There's no time to think. You have to say something now.
text.B2: You reach her, and your heart turns right over. It's Cass — your sister, older now, the same tired eyes, a packed bag at her feet. She came. The one you fell out with, years ago, and never once put right. There's no time to stop and think. You have to say something, and say it now.

text.A2: You say her name across the yard, and for a moment there's nothing. Then she turns, and her face changes — surprise, then something softer, harder to read. 'It's you,' she says. And you hear how much is in those two words.
text.B1: You say her name across the yard, and for a moment there's nothing at all. Then she turns, and her face changes — surprise, then something softer, harder to read. 'It's you,' she says. And you can hear how much is in those two words.

text.A2: You face Cass at last, and all the years come up between you. Slowly, the stiffness in her shoulders eases. She looks past you at the van. 'Mum's really going, then,' she says quietly. 'Let me help carry.' Even now, she's thinking of Mum, and the door home.

text.A2: Cass looks at you, her eyes clearer now. 'We stopped talking after Dad,' she says. 'Too much said, too much not said. My fault as much as yours. It's a long, sad story.' And you hear just how long it is.

text.A2: You decide to clear the air before the light goes. You and Cass, after all these years apart. It's a small thing, next to the whole day's weight. But it's not nothing. Some shut doors can still be opened.

text.A2: The figure stands still, and your nerve works at you, slow and cruel. And yet they came all this way, to your gate, on today of all days. You can't just carry on and pretend. You have to go closer and be sure who it is.

text.A2: You go closer, and you know her at once. It's Cass — your own sister, not seen in years, not since the day it all fell apart. Then she looks up and sees you too. There's no hiding now.

text.A2: Bray swings by one last time, engine running. 'Still at it the hard way?' he says. 'Give it up. Let me finish it off — last chance, cash, done by dark.' The same easy smile. The same old con.

text.A2: You're at the new flat at last, arms dead, the last load at the kerb. The dark is almost here. Inside, the rooms are bare and cold, waiting to be filled. Mum sits in the van, wrapped up, trusting you. This is the moment it all rests on. Everything now comes down to what you do next.

text.A2: Then help takes the weight at last. Cass at one end, a neighbour at the other — hands you didn't have an hour ago. You're not carrying it alone now. Others are here to share the load. It's like setting down something heavy you'd carried too far, too long.

text.A2: The full van does it. You carry in the bed, the chair, the boxes, and the bare rooms start to fill. A lamp goes on. The place warms and softens against the dark window. This, you think, is what a home is made of.

text.A2: You've not much left in the van, so you make every trip count. The bed, the chair, one box of Mum's things, and a lot of care. You carry the important things first. It's bare, and plain. It may be enough for tonight — or it may not.

text.A2: What's in is thin, and you're afraid it won't do for tonight. You've carried all you can on your own. But the rooms still feel empty and cold. You need more now — more hands, more trips, or both.

text.A2: You glance back at the gate and see it. There, by the wall, that figure again — still, half-turned, waiting. It's where no one you'd expect would be. It pulls at your eye. And it pulls at something deeper than that.

text.A2: The figure at the gate stands again. It stands where you'd swear no one you knew would be. But a face you half know means a story. A story means a choice. A person right there, from your past, on today of all days.

text.A2: Now comes the last long haul. You carry, you climb, you set things down, and watch the light drop over the roofs. It's not easy — just steady, heavy, tiring work. But it's the whole job now. And it's yours to do.

text.A2: And then, at last, it turns. The van is nearly empty. The bed is up, the chair's by the window, the kettle's found. It's almost dark now. You've nearly got the whole move done.

text.A2: You look down the street from the new door. Warm windows glow all along the row. Other homes, other families, other lives behind the glass. This is your row now, and your light's going on too. You were never quite as alone as you felt.

text.A2: At last, the last of it comes in. Cass and a neighbour carry Mum's chair between them, and you bring her in on your arm. You stand in the new hall, your legs shaking under you now. But the worst of the day is behind you.

text.A2: And what does the day leave you with? Maybe not a perfect move. Maybe just the fact that you tried, that you kept carrying. When your back ached and the light went and it was easy to stop, you didn't. That counts for something.

text.A2: There was no quick fix — there was something far better. You turned a street of strangers into a chain of hands on the stairs. One carried, one packed, one kept Mum company at the window. Together you got it all in before dark. No one did it alone today, and the block won't forget who started it.
